extracted.intended_audience: debt collectors, compliance officers, and legal counsel interpreting FDCPA/CFPB communication rules
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and interpretive commentary on permissible and prohibited communications by debt collectors under CFPB regulations implementing the FDCPA, including rules for electronic communications, communications with represented consumers, workplace contacts, opt-outs, location information, and harassing or abusive conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer-initiated communications when represented by an attorney
rubrics_metrics.description: A consumer-initiated communication from a consumer represented by an attorney constitutes the consumer's prior consent to that communication under § 1006.6(b)(4)(i); therefore, a debt collector may respond to that consumer-initiated communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The consumer's act of initiating does not negate the debt collector's knowledge that the consumer is represented and does not revoke protections under § 1006.6(b)(2). After responding, the debt collector must not further communicate with the consumer unless the debt collector knows the consumer is not represented with respect to the debt (based on information from the consumer or the consumer's attorney), or an exception under § 1006.6(b)(2)(i) or (ii) or § 1006.6(b)(4) applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communications at consumer's place of employment
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1006.6(b)(3) prohibits a debt collector from communicating or attempting to communicate with a consumer at the consumer's place of employment if the debt collector knows or has reason to know the employer prohibits such communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A debt collector 'knows or has reason to know' an employer prohibits contact if, for example, the consumer tells the collector they cannot take personal calls at work. The collector may ask follow-up questions to clarify employer prohibitions or limitations. See also special rules for employer-provided email at § 1006.22(f)(3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior consent — general limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Under § 1006.6(b)(4)(i), prohibitions in § 1006.6(b)(1)–(3) do not apply if the collector has the prior consent of the consumer to communicate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the collector learns during a communication that the consumer is at an inconvenient time/place, the collector may ask what would be convenient but may not ask the consumer to consent to continuation of the inconvenient communication. Prior consent must be given directly to the debt collector (not to a creditor or previous collector).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior consent must be given directly to the debt collector
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1006.6(b)(4)(i) requires prior consent to be given directly to the debt collector; consent given to a creditor or previous debt collector cannot be relied on by the current debt collector.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct consent may be provided through any medium of communication (writing, electronic, or oral).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer-provided email treated as consent if disclosure provided
rubrics_metrics.description: If a consumer provides an email address to a debt collector (including on the collector's website or portal), the collector may treat that as consent to use the address if the collector 'discloses clearly and conspicuously' that it may use the email to communicate about the debt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure must be clear and conspicuous; consent may be provided through any medium. See related creditor-based notice procedures at § 1006.6(d)(4)(ii).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions for mortgage servicers — written early intervention notice
rubrics_metrics.description: The Bureau interprets the written early intervention notice required by 12 CFR 1024.39(d)(3) to fall within the exceptions to the cease communication provision in FDCPA § 805(c)(2) and (3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 12 CFR 1024.39(d)(3), its commentary, and the Bureau's 2016 FDCPA Interpretive Rule (81 FR 71977 (Oct. 19, 2016)) for implementation guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mortgage servicing rule compliance not FDCPA liability
rubrics_metrics.description: Notwithstanding a consumer's cease communication request, a mortgage servicer subject to the FDCPA is not liable under the FDCPA for complying with certain servicing rule provisions (e.g., required disclosures about forced-place insurance, ARM initial interest rate adjustment, periodic statements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 12 CFR 1024.37, 1026.20(d), and 1026.41 and CFPB Bulletin 2013-12 (Oct. 15, 2013) for implementation guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge that electronic communication caused prohibited disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: For § 1006.6(d)(3)(ii), a debt collector 'knows' that sending an email/text led to a prohibited disclosure if any person has informed the debt collector of that fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If informed, the collector must treat that address/number as having led to a disclosure prohibited by § 1006.6(d)(1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedures for emails based on consumer-debt collector communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Under § 1006.6(d)(4)(i)(B), a debt collector may send email to an address if the collector received directly from the consumer prior consent to use that email address to communicate about the debt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consent may be provided through any medium (written, electronic, oral). If the consumer provided the email (including via the collector's website), the collector may treat it as consent if the collector clearly and conspicuously disclosed potential use of the email to communicate about the debt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedures for emails based on creditor communications
rubrics_metrics.description: Under § 1006.6(d)(4)(ii)(B)–(C), a debt collector may send email if the creditor used the email to communicate about the account and the creditor sent a clear and conspicuous notice disclosing transfer to the collector, possible use of email by the collector, opt-out instructions, and deadline to opt out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communications about the account include required disclosures, bills, invoices, statements, payment reminders/confirmations; do not include marketing. The notice may be combined with larger communications if still clear and conspicuous. Sample written and electronic language is provided in the commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of the debt collector in creditor notice
rubrics_metrics.description: The notice provided by the creditor must clearly and conspicuously identify the specific debt collector to which the debt has been or will be transferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to identify the specific debt collector would not satisfy § 1006.6(d)(4)(ii)(C)(1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable and simple method to opt out required in creditor notice
rubrics_metrics.description: The creditor's notice must clearly and conspicuously disclose instructions for a reasonable and simple method by which the consumer can opt out of the debt collector's use of the email address to communicate about the debt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: For written notice, include a reply form and pre-addressed envelope with the opt-out notice; requiring the consumer to call or write to obtain a form does not meet the requirement. For electronic notice, provide an electronic means like a hyperlink or allow replying 'stop'; requiring postal mail/phone without a link does not meet the requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opt-out receipt deadline — at least 35 days
rubrics_metrics.description: The creditor's notice must disclose the date by which a debt collector or creditor must receive a consumer's request to opt out, which must be at least 35 days after the date the notice is sent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notice may instruct the consumer to respond to the debt collector or the creditor but not to both; the recipient must be specified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of opt-out request after expiration of opt-out period
rubrics_metrics.description: If a consumer requests after the expiration of the opt-out period that the debt collector not communicate using the email address identified in the opt-out notice, § 1006.14(h)(1) prohibits the debt collector from communicating or attempting to communicate with the consumer using that email address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the consumer requests after the expiration that the collector not communicate by email, § 1006.14(h)(1) prohibits future email communication, including use of that specific address. If the consumer also notifies the collector in writing/electronically that the consumer refuses to pay or wants the collector to cease communication, § 1006.6(c)(1) prohibits further communication subject to exceptions in §1006.6(c)(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of opt-out request — not a general cease communication
rubrics_metrics.description: A consumer's request to opt out of a debt collector's use of a particular email address does not constitute a notification to cease further communication with respect to the debt under § 1006.6(c)(1), absent evidence that the consumer refuses to pay or wants the collector to cease all communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opt-out of an address is narrower than a § 1006.6(c)(1) cease-communication notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain name available for public use
rubrics_metrics.description: Under § 1006.6(d)(4)(ii)(E), a domain name of an email address is 'available for use by the general public' when multiple members of the public are permitted to use the same domain (free or paid).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Domain names reserved for particular registrants (e.g., branded corporate domains or .gov/.edu/.org reserved types) are not 'available for use by the general public.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of employer-provided email address
rubrics_metrics.description: For § 1006.6(d)(4)(ii)(E), a debt collector knows an email address is employer-provided if any person has informed the collector that the address is employer-provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collectors are not required to conduct a manual review of consumer accounts to determine whether an email address might be employer-provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communications based on immediately prior debt collector's use
rubrics_metrics.description: Under § 1006.6(d)(4)(iii), a debt collector may send email if the immediately prior debt collector used the email address to communicate with the consumer about the debt; this may give the current collector a bona fide error defense to civil liability for unintentional third-party disclosure if the prior collector obtained the email in accordance with §§ 1006.6(d)(4)(i) or (ii) and the consumer did not opt out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'immediately prior debt collector' is the collector immediately preceding the current one. Examples illustrate chains of transfers where the defense does or does not apply depending on whether the immediately prior collector used email.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telephone numbers for text messages — database confirmation
rubrics_metrics.description: Under § 1006.6(d)(5)(i) and (ii), a debt collector may send a text message to a telephone number if the collector confirms, using a complete and accurate database, that the telephone number has not been reassigned from the consumer to another user.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The FCC database established in In re Advanced Methods to Target & Eliminate Unlawful Robocalls (33 FCC Rcd. 12024 (Dec. 12, 2018)) qualifies as a complete and accurate database; substantially similar commercial databases also qualify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text messaging allowed when consumer texted collector
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1006.6(d)(5)(i) permits sending a text message if the consumer used the telephone number to communicate by text message with the debt collector about the debt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision does not apply if the consumer used the telephone number only to communicate by voice call with the debt collector.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opt-in/prior consent guidance for text messages
rubrics_metrics.description: See guidance in comment 6(d)(4)(i)(B) concerning how a consumer may provide prior consent directly to a debt collector and when a provided telephone number may be treated as consent for text messages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior consent may be provided through any medium; consumer-provided numbers may be treated as consent if collector disclosed intended use clearly and conspicuously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opt-out notice requirement for electronic communications (§1006.6(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1006.6(e) requires that a debt collector who communicates or attempts to communicate electronically using a specific email address or telephone number for texts include a clear and conspicuous statement describing a reasonable and simple method by which the consumer can opt out of further electronic communications to that address or number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Reply STOP' in a text; a hyperlink labeled 'Click here to opt out' in an email; or instructions to reply with 'stop' in the subject line — each is acceptable if readily noticeable and legible. No minimum type size is mandated. See comments for meanings of 'clear and conspicuous' and 'reasonable and simple.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Location information: communications with third parties about a deceased consumer
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1006.10(b)(2) prohibits a debt collector communicating with anyone other than the consumer for location information from stating that the consumer owes any debt. If the consumer is deceased and the collector is seeking the person authorized to act on behalf of the estate, the collector may state it is seeking to identify and locate that person or the person handling the financial affairs of the deceased consumer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If seeking an executor/administrator/personal representative of a deceased consumer's estate, the collector may describe the purpose as locating the person authorized to act for the estate. See § 1006.6(a)(4) commentary for more on executors/administrators/personal representatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: General prohibition on harassing, oppressive, or abusive conduct (§1006.14(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1006.14(a) prohibits a debt collector from engaging in any conduct the natural consequence of which is to harass, oppress, or abuse any person in connection with the collection of a debt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This covers specific conduct in §§ 1006.14(b)–(h) and other conduct whose natural consequence is harassment, oppression, or abuse, regardless of medium (in-person, phone, recordings, paper, mail, email, text, social media, etc.). Example: numerous unsolicited text messages per day over several days likely violate §1006.14(a) even if no specific prohibition in (b)–(h) is triggered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cumulative effect of communications
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether conduct violates § 1006.14(a) may depend on the cumulative effect of the debt collector's conduct across any communication media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct that alone might not violate §1006.14(a) or specific prohibitions could nonetheless violate §1006.14(a) when evaluated cumulatively with other conduct (e.g., multiple phone calls plus multiple emails).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on repeated or continuous telephone calls (§1006.14(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1006.14(b) prohibits placing telephone calls or engaging any person in telephone conversations repeatedly or continuously with intent to annoy, abuse, or harass, and describes presumptions of compliance or violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Placing a telephone call' includes conveying a ringless voicemail but does not include sending an electronic message (e.g., text or email) that may be received on a mobile phone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of compliance with telephone-frequency rule
rubrics_metrics.description: A debt collector who complies with § 1006.14(b)(1) and FDCPA §1692d(5) complies with §1006.14(a) and FDCPA §1692d solely with respect to the frequency of telephone calls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compliance with frequency does not shield the collector from violations based on other aspects of calls (e.g., obscene voicemail content could still violate §1006.14(a) and (d)). See comment example of obscene voicemail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telephone call frequencies and presumptions (§1006.14(b)(2)(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: A debt collector is presumed to comply if it places a call to a person in connection with a debt no more than seven times within seven consecutive days and does not place a call within seven consecutive days after having a telephone conversation with the person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both prongs must not be exceeded for the presumption to apply. Telephone call frequencies are subject to exclusions in §1006.14(b)(3). For (b)(2)(i)(B), the date of the telephone conversation is the first day of the seven-consecutive-day period. Examples illustrate counting and timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors that may rebut the presumption of compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: To rebut the presumption of compliance under §1006.14(b)(2)(i), factors may show that the collector placed calls repeatedly or continuously with intent to annoy, abuse, or harass despite frequency limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-exhaustive factors (considered individually or together): (i) frequency and pattern of calls (e.g., calls in rapid succession or highly concentrated within a day); (ii) frequency and pattern of voicemails; (iii) content of the person's prior communications (e.g., told collector not to contact, refusing to pay, dispute of debt, or a cease-communication notification); (iv) the collector's conduct in prior communications (e.g., obscene/profane language, threats, calling at inconvenient times). The amount of time since prior communications may also be relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption still applies to misdirected telephone calls if within frequency limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1006.14(b)(2)(i) provides that a debt collector is presumed to comply with frequency limits if its telephone call frequencies do not exceed the described limits, even where calls are misdirected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See § 1006.10(c) for further guidance on communicating with persons other than the consumer for acquiring location information.
